analysis.one_liner: Bans large meatpackers from owning or feeding the livestock they slaughter.
analysis.headline: Despite bipartisan sponsorship from farm-state senators, the bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Large meatpacking companies increasingly own or contract-feed the cattle, hogs, and other animals they slaughter, meaning the company controls the animal from birth to meat counter. This bill would make it illegal for a packer to own, feed, or control slaughter-bound livestock so completely that the farmer running the operation no longer has a real say. Small packers, farmer-owned cooperatives, and short-term arrangements in the final week before slaughter would be exempt. The bill went to the Senate Agriculture Committee on day one of the 108th Congress and stayed there.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent livestock farmers and ranchers, who would regain leverage in selling their animals. When a packer owns the livestock itself, it does not have to bid against anyone for the farmer's animals, which pushes down the prices farmers receive and hides how the market really works.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a packer to own, feed, or control livestock intended for slaughter to the extent that the farmer is no longer materially participating in managing the operation [S2] [S3].

The ban covers ownership through subsidiaries and through arrangements that give the packer operational, managerial, or supervisory control over the livestock or the farming operation, closing the most common routes around it [S3].
The ban takes effect quickly for existing violations — within 180 days for cattle and other livestock, and within 18 months for hogs — so packers could not simply wait it out [S3].

Carve-outs protect small and farmer-owned players: cooperatives majority-owned by active members who supply the livestock, packers too small to report daily price and quantity data, and packers that own only one processing plant [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies, which would have to unwind packer-owned feeding operations and buy animals on the open market from independent producers instead of supplying themselves.

drawbacks.text: The exemptions are substantial: cooperatives, single-plant packers, and packers below the daily reporting threshold are all carved out, and arrangements made within seven days of slaughter remain legal — loopholes a determined integrator could build around [S2] [S3].

The bill changes market structure but does not create a new enforcement mechanism beyond the Packers and Stockyards Act itself, so its real-world bite would depend on how aggressively the Agriculture Department polices the new prohibition [S3].

Packers argue that owning livestock lets them guarantee a steady, uniform supply and consistent quality; a good-faith objection is that unwinding vertical integration could raise packers' costs and, eventually, meat prices for consumers. The bill's backers contend the current system's bidding distortion costs farmers far more.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: packers lose the ability to control their own supply and squeeze farmers on price, while consumers take on some risk of higher packer costs being passed through. The exemption structure is the weak point — it was broad enough that well-advised companies could likely have preserved much of their integration — so even if enacted, the bill's benefits would have depended heavily on regulation and litigation. It never got that far, because it never got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 108th Congress and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it sat without a hearing or a vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on January 7, 2003, joined by Sens. Tim Johnson, Mike Enzi, and Tom Harkin [S3] [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry; that is the last action recorded for the bill in the 108th Congress [S5] [S1].
The committee never reported the bill, so it never reached the Senate floor or the House, and it died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies that own and feed livestock ahead of slaughter keep the integrated supply arrangements the bill would have unwound, and independent producers keep competing against their own buyers' captive supply. Consumers see no change either way.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 7, 2003 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the remaining two years of the Congress [S5] [S1].

against.name: Major meatpacking and livestock-industry interests
against.what_they_did: Industry groups and large packing companies opposed federal restrictions on packer ownership of livestock throughout this period, arguing vertical integration secures supply and quality.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: Grassley (R-IA) introduced it with a Democrat and a Republican as original cosponsors, and the eventual cosponsor list was 5 Democrats and 1 Republican; no votes were ever taken, so no party split ever appeared on the record [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill would force packers to divest ownership and control of slaughter-bound livestock and buy animals on the open market, ending the captive-supply arrangement that lets them pay farmers less. Packers' cost savings come largely at independent producers' expense.

industries.industry: Livestock cooperatives owned by active farmer members
industries.note: Cooperatives majority-owned by active members who supply their own livestock are exempt, so farmer-owned slaughter capacity is protected and would gain relative advantage over packer-owned integration.
Packers below the daily price-reporting threshold or owning one plant are exempt from the ban, leaving them free to integrate vertically while larger competitors cannot.
